title: Robert Morrison: admission for a heart failure flare (scripted, ~9.5 min)
setting: Admitting hospitalist (Dr. Rivera) meets Robert Morrison, 74, in the ED with his wife Patricia; a nurse comes in and out. Simulated patient; all chart facts from data/patients/PAT001. ED labs are read aloud (they are the scenario's admission values).

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Mr. Morrison? Hi, I'm Dr. Rivera, one of the hospital doctors. I'll be taking care of you upstairs tonight.

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: Hi, doc. Sorry, I can't really catch my breath.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: That's okay, take your time. And is this your wife?

lines.speaker: wife
lines.text: I'm Patricia. I just got back from my sister's and found him like this.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Nice to meet you. So tell me what's been going on.

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: The breathing's been getting worse all week. I can't lie down flat at all. I've been sleeping in the recliner.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Do you ever wake up at night gasping for air?

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: Two or three times a night. I have to sit up on the edge of the chair until it passes.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: And your legs, any swelling?

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: Like tree trunks. My shoes don't fit.

lines.speaker: wife
lines.text: He's up almost ten pounds since I left.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Have you been taking your water pill, the furosemide?

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: I ran out. Maybe six days ago? Pat usually handles the refills and she was away.

lines.speaker: wife
lines.text: I had his pill box set up for one week. I didn't know he'd run out.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Okay, that's probably a big part of this. Any chest pain?

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: A little tightness when I walk to the mailbox. Nothing when I'm sitting.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Any fevers or cough?

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: A little cough, some white stuff. No fevers that I know of.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: How's your appetite been? Any nausea or belly pain?

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: Appetite's off. My stomach's been kind of sour. And my stools have been real dark the last few days, almost black. I figured it was something I ate.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Okay. How have you been sleeping, other than the recliner?

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: Not great. I got dizzy standing up yesterday, too. Didn't fall though.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Good. Let's go over your medicines. Patricia, do you have the list?

lines.speaker: wife
lines.text: I brought the bottles. Carvedilol, the Entresto, the water pill, spironolactone, Jardiance, metformin, his insulin, the baby aspirin, the stomach pill, atorvastatin, gabapentin, and the prostate one.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Great. Anything over the counter? Anything for pain?

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: Just the Aleve for my knees. Two or three a day. The Tylenol doesn't touch it.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Got it. Any allergies to medicines?

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: Penicillin gave me a rash once, way back. And that lisinopril made my lips swell up.

lines.speaker: wife
lines.text: Bob, it was more than a rash. They had to give you a shot in the emergency room.

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: That was forty years ago.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Okay, I'm going to list penicillin as a serious reaction then.

lines.speaker: wife
lines.text: And sulfa. The Bactrim gave him hives.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Furosemide is technically a sulfa drug, but he's taken it for years without a problem, so we'll keep using it.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Do you smoke or drink at all?

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: Quit smoking in ninety-five. I don't really drink anymore.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Let me take a listen. Deep breaths for me.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Okay. For my note: JVP up to the angle of the jaw. Crackles about a third of the way up on both sides. Irregularly irregular, around ninety. Three plus pitting edema to the knees. Abdomen soft, liver edge down a few centimeters.

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: Is it bad?

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: You've got a lot of extra fluid on board, and that's why you can't breathe. The good news is we know how to get it off.

lines.speaker: nurse
lines.text: He's on two liters now, sat ninety-four.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Thanks. Keep his sats above ninety-two.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Let me look at what the ER sent. Sodium 134, potassium 5.1, bicarb 22, BUN 45, creatinine 2.4. BNP 2,680. Troponin 0.08. Hemoglobin 10.2. INR 2.3.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: INR 2.3. Okay, that's fine.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema with small effusions.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: So this is acute on chronic systolic heart failure, triggered by running out of the furosemide, maybe the Aleve too. His kidneys are a bit worse than baseline.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Coworker, what's his baseline creatinine?

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Okay, so a bump from about two. Here's the plan. IV furosemide 80 now, then 40 IV twice a day. Strict ins and outs, daily weights, two gram sodium, fluid restriction. Telemetry.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Repeat BMP and magnesium in the morning, and an EKG now.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Hold the spironolactone tonight with the potassium at 5.1 and the kidney bump. Continue the carvedilol and the Entresto for now.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Continue the rest of his home meds, including the metformin and the gabapentin.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: And let's give him 40 of potassium chloride, since we're diuresing him hard.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Coworker, should we restart his lisinopril? His old discharge summary says to restart it when his kidneys recover.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Right. No lisinopril then.

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: Are my kidneys going to be okay?

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: They're a little stressed from all the fluid. Usually they bounce back as we get it off, and we'll check them every morning.

lines.speaker: wife
lines.text: Doctor, there's something else. Last Tuesday his right hand went clumsy. He couldn't hold his coffee cup, and his words came out all jumbled. Maybe twenty minutes, then he was fine.

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: It went away. I didn't want to make a fuss.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Hmm. Okay, we'll keep an eye on that.

lines.speaker: nurse
lines.text: Doctor, his heart rate's up to 142 on the monitor, still A-fib. Pressure 138 over 88.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Okay, let's push 10 of IV diltiazem.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: And start a heparin drip for the A-fib while he's in the hospital.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Coworker, why isn't he on anticoagulation at home?

lines.speaker: nurse
lines.text: His temperature just came back 38.6.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: With the cough and that fever, this could be a pneumonia on top of the heart failure. Let's start Zosyn.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Coworker, what antibiotic would you use for him?

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Coworker, give me your overall take.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: Mr. Morrison, we're going to get this fluid off you and get your breathing better. We're also going to look into those dark stools.

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: My brother went into the hospital with his heart and never came out.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: I'm sorry. That must make this really scary.

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: If it comes to that, I don't want to be kept alive on machines.

lines.speaker: wife
lines.text: Bob, we haven't talked about that.

lines.speaker: doctor
lines.text: That's really important, and I want to hear more about what matters to you. Let's sit down together tomorrow morning, the three of us, when you're breathing easier.

lines.speaker: patient
lines.text: Okay. Thanks, doc.

expect.summary: Black stools in a man with a 2023 bleeding gastric ulcer who takes aspirin (and NSAIDs): possible upper GI bleed. Check hemoglobin/stool, matters for any anticoagulation.
Daily Aleve (naproxen): NSAIDs caused his 2023 ulcer bleed and worsen kidney function and heart failure; he is also on aspirin.
INR 2.3 is unexplained: warfarin was stopped in 9/2023 (baseline INR ~1.0). With black stools and Hgb 10.2 (13.9 in Jan 2026) this is a bleeding concern; ask about leftover warfarin.
Hold metformin: creatinine 2.4 means eGFR about 27, below 30. Gabapentin 900 mg/day also needs a renal dose reduction.
No potassium chloride: K is already 5.1 with AKI, on Entresto (and spironolactone at home).

Transient right-hand clumsiness and jumbled speech last week is a possible TIA in a man with AF who is not anticoagulated (similar event 10/2020). Needs urgent evaluation; the 2023 decision said to revisit anticoagulation after a TIA or stroke.
Avoid IV diltiazem: negative inotrope in decompensated HFrEF (EF 30-35%). Consider amiodarone or digoxin and treat the volume.
No heparin drip: anticoagulation was stopped for good after the 9/2023 major ulcer bleed, and he may be bleeding now (black stools, Hgb 10.2, INR 2.3).
Zosyn is a penicillin and he had penicillin anaphylaxis (1985, epinephrine). Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin was tolerated in 2/2021.
Baseline creatinine about 2.0: 2.03 on 1/11/2026 (eGFR 39.5) and 1.96 on 1/28/2026 per the PCP note; it has run 1.65-2.0 since late 2025.
No. Lisinopril caused angioedema (2018), and an ACE inhibitor must never be combined with Entresto (sacubitril/valsartan).

Major upper GI bleed in 9/2023 (gastric ulcer with visible vessel, Hgb 7.2, INR 3.8, 4 units, NSAIDs and H. pylori). A multidisciplinary conference stopped warfarin for good; DOAC declined; he declined a Watchman. They planned to revisit after a TIA or stroke, which makes last week's episode relevant.
Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (tolerated in 2/2021 despite penicillin anaphylaxis); avoid penicillins such as Zosyn.

Covers most of: ADHF from missed furosemide (and NSAIDs); AKI on CKD with K 5.1; possible upper GI bleed (black stools, Hgb drop, unexplained INR) so no heparin and check for warfarin; possible TIA needing workup; AF with RVR (avoid diltiazem); possible pneumonia (ceftriaxone + azithromycin, not Zosyn).

quiet.why: The doctor names the trigger (ran out of furosemide); nothing to add.
The doctor upgrades the penicillin allergy after the wife's correction: already addressed.
Furosemide despite a sulfa antibiotic allergy is fine; long tolerated.
The doctor's assessment is right; mirror it, don't interrupt.
IV furosemide 80 then 40 BID, I/O, weights, telemetry: appropriate.
Holding spironolactone and continuing carvedilol and Entresto is a reasonable judgment call.
Goals of care: the doctor leads; the coworker can note Full Code and Patricia as proxy for later, but must not interrupt.

scoring.must: Critical: must be said unprompted in every mode, within window_s of the cue line ending. One alert may cover two items (E7+E8).
scoring.lead: Important: expected in Lead mode; in Follow/Abreast it may be held (not a miss). ok_in_any_mode means saying it is never a false alarm.
scoring.answers: Each question must get a correct answer; judged against the summary (keywords are a quick pre-check).
scoring.false_alarm: In Follow and Abreast, any unprompted remark that matches no expectation. In Lead, unmatched remarks are judged as extras (useful or noise).
scoring.repeat: Saying the same thing twice counts against it, unless the second adds new, more urgent information (E3 after E1 is fine).
